title: How does seasonal weather affect construction employment?
gist: Using BLS state construction payrolls from May 2016 to June 2026, the FRED Blog shows that Minnesota's construction employment has a far wider seasonal swing than Kentucky's — both peak in August and trough in February, but the cold-winter state's amplitude is much larger — and argues the gap reflects the South's ability to keep building through winter. The practical trick is normalizing the seasonal gap as a fraction of seasonally adjusted employment so states of very different size become comparable.

insights.claim: Construction employment in Minnesota and Kentucky follows the same seasonal shape — rising through August and declining until February — so the seasonal turning points in state construction payrolls are calendar-stable regardless of latitude.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Anyone reading monthly state construction payroll prints should expect an August high and February low as the baseline; deviations from that calendar are the actual news.
insights.quote: increases through August and declines until February
insights.locator: To better tell the story behind

insights.claim: Measured as a fraction of seasonally adjusted employment, the seasonal swing in construction employment is much larger in Minnesota than in Kentucky — much higher highs and much lower lows — over May 2016 to June 2026.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Cold-state construction data carries far more seasonal noise, so the same unadjusted month-over-month move means very different things in Minnesota versus Kentucky.
insights.quote: a much wider seasonal range in Minnesota than in Kentucky. (That is, much higher highs and much lower lows for Minnesota.)
insights.locator: To better tell the story behind

insights.claim: The FRED Blog attributes the wider seasonal employment range in northern states to the fact that southern winters allow construction work to continue through more of the year, making weather the proposed mechanism behind cross-state seasonality differences.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: If weather is the driver, warming winters or unusually mild/severe seasons should compress or widen northern construction payroll swings — a testable overlay for regional homebuilder and materials demand.
insights.quote: This difference could be related to the ability to work through more of the winter months in the South relative to the North.
insights.locator: To better tell the story behind

insights.claim: Seasonal employment concentration is not unique to construction: FRED has previously documented that retail and postal services employment peaks around the Christmas holidays, indicating seasonality analysis generalizes across labor-intensive, calendar-driven industries.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: The same seasonal-amplitude method can be pointed at retail and logistics payrolls to separate genuine cycle inflections from calendar effects.

insights.claim: Comparing raw construction employment peaks and troughs across states is unreliable because absolute headcount differences swamp seasonal signal — Minnesota has far more construction employees than Kentucky simply because it is more populous.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Level comparisons across states are a trap; scale-invariant measures are required before drawing conclusions about regional labor-market strength.
insights.quote: comparing annual employment peaks and throughs between states isn’t easy or straightforward
insights.locator: Note there are far more construction employees

insights.claim: The fix for size-distorted comparisons is to plot the seasonal component — the gap between unadjusted and seasonally adjusted employment — as a fraction of seasonally adjusted employment, which renders seasonality comparable across states of different sizes.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: A reusable, cheap normalization for any regional or sector series where the base sizes differ — apply it before ranking states or industries on cyclical volatility.
insights.quote: the size of the seasonal changes in employment as a fraction of the seasonally adjusted employment figures
insights.locator: To better tell the story behind

insights.claim: The analysis rests on a 2018 research piece from the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago on why construction employment follows different patterns across states, giving the weather-seasonality argument a prior research anchor rather than being a novel finding.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Points to a deeper source for anyone building a formal model of regional construction seasonality.
insights.locator: The FRED Blog has discussed why employment

insights.claim: The exact FRED series for replicating state construction seasonality are MNCONS and KYCONS (seasonally adjusted) paired with MNCONSN and KYCONSN (not seasonally adjusted) for All Employees: Construction in Minnesota and Kentucky, with state-level employment by industry available across FRED.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Gives a ready-made ticker recipe to extend the seasonal-amplitude screen to all 50 states and other industries without hunting for series IDs.
